idiom_name: (a, b) switch { (Circle c, Square s) => ..., _ => throw ... }
implementation_notes: C# resolves the pair in one construct: a switch expression over the tuple (a, b) with type patterns matches both runtime types at once, and inside the arm both operands are already narrowed, so no casts and no visitor round-trip are needed. Pattern matching replaces the classic accept/visit structure for hierarchies you own, and records plus sealed hierarchies let the compiler reason about the closed set. Runtime dispatch of the same kind is available through the DLR (dynamic) - see the dynamic-dispatch variant - while the classic visitor stays the answer for hierarchies extended by third parties.
pitfalls: Arms match in order and a discarded `_ =>` arm turns a missing pair into silent wrong behaviour: make the fallback throw.
Records give value equality, not closed hierarchies; seal the base type so the compiler can reason about completeness.
The `dynamic` alternative re-runs the binder per type pair and reports ambiguity as a runtime exception instead of a compile error.

variants.name: Classic Visitor with Accept/Visit (two virtual calls)
variants.implementation_notes: The GoF structure maps onto interfaces: each element implements Accept by calling the visitor method for its own type, so the element axis is resolved by interface dispatch and the operation axis by the visitor's runtime type. Adding an element type breaks every visitor at compile time, which is the guarantee the pattern sells; the same shape drives Roslyn's syntax visitors. Use it when the element hierarchy is owned by someone else, when operations are the unit of testing, or when the visitor must be enumerable by reflection (plug-in systems).
pitfalls: A Visit(Shape) method makes new element types compile silently: omit the base overload deliberately.
Async operations do not fit a synchronous visitor interface: declare Task-returning visit methods from the start or use pattern matching.
Interfaces expose every operation to the element class: keep the visitor in a separate assembly when the data model must not depend on the operation set.

variants.name: DLR multiple dispatch with dynamic
variants.idiom_name: dynamic operands + overload set resolved at runtime
variants.implementation_notes: Casting both operands to dynamic defers overload resolution to the DLR, which picks the most specific method for the actual runtime types - real multiple dispatch with no visitor boilerplate and no accept methods, and call sites are cached after the first resolution. It is the shortest route for rule sets that grow by adding overloads, but coverage is no longer checked: a missing pair resolves to a base-type overload or throws RuntimeBinderException, so a throwing base overload is mandatory.
pitfalls: Two candidate overloads that are equally specific (e.g. differing in two unrelated axes) become a RuntimeBinderException instead of a compile error.
The DLR caches every (type-pair, call-site) combination: an unbounded set of runtime types grows the cache for the process lifetime.
dynamic disables static checking of the whole call chain it touches, so typos surface at runtime only.
